tracks.title: Spot the Typo
tracks.summary: Syntax errors: the code won't even run yet.
tracks.intro_md: Every puzzle here fails before it even starts. You'll learn to read `SyntaxError` and `IndentationError` messages and fix the shape of the code, not its logic.

tracks.title: Crash Course
tracks.summary: Runtime errors: the code runs, then crashes partway through.
tracks.intro_md: These puzzles run until something goes wrong. You'll learn to read a traceback from the bottom up and recognise what each exception type is telling you.

tracks.title: Wrong Answer
tracks.summary: The code runs fine and gives you a confidently wrong answer.
tracks.intro_md: No errors here - just the wrong result. You'll compare expected vs actual output and get used to checking boundary values by hand.

tracks.title: Deep Bugs
tracks.summary: Subtler logic bugs that need a trace table to really see.
tracks.intro_md: These bugs hide in state, scope and recursion. You'll use trace tables and variable watch to see what's really happening, step by step.

tracks.title: Boss Fights
tracks.summary: Bigger programs with more than one bug hiding in them.
tracks.intro_md: Multiple bugs, longer code. You'll divide and conquer, build minimal examples, and work the full debugging loop end to end.

concepts.title: Colons and blocks
concepts.summary: Every block header (if, for, while, def, class...) ends in a colon.
concepts.lesson_md:
## What it is

Any line that starts an indented block - `if`, `elif`, `else`, `for`, `while`, `def`, `class`, `try`, `except` - must end with a colon `:`.

## What it looks like when it goes wrong

```
SyntaxError: expected ':'
```

Python points at the end of the line that's missing it.

## How to spot it

Scan every line that should open a block. Does it end in `:`? It's an easy thing to miss because the line still *looks* finished without one.

## How to fix it

Add the colon at the end of the header line, before the indented block starts.

## Try it

```python run
for i in range(3):
    print(i)
```

concepts.title: Names and scope
concepts.summary: Python only knows a name once something has assigned it, spelled exactly.
concepts.lesson_md:
## What it is

A name (variable, function, parameter) only exists once it's been created, and Python matches names exactly, including capitalisation.

## What it looks like when it goes wrong

```
NameError: name 'nmae' is not defined
```

## How to spot it

Compare the name in the error to every place that name is created or passed in - letter by letter.

## How to fix it

Fix the spelling (or capitalisation) so it matches exactly everywhere it's used.

## Try it

```python run
name = "Ada"
print("Hello, " + name)
```

concepts.title: Off-by-one errors
concepts.summary: Loops and ranges that stop one step too early or too late.
concepts.lesson_md:
## What it is

A loop, range or boundary check that's out by exactly one - the most common logic bug in programming.

## What it looks like when it goes wrong

No error at all - just a result that's slightly wrong, often missing the first or last item.

## How to spot it

Test with the smallest possible input by hand (n = 1, or an empty list) and check the first and last values a loop actually touches.

## How to fix it

Adjust the range, the comparison operator (< vs <=), or the starting value so the boundary is included (or excluded) correctly.

## Try it

```python run
for i in range(1, 5):
    print(i)
```

concepts.title: How range() works
concepts.summary: range(a, b) includes a but stops before b.
concepts.lesson_md:
## What it is

`range(a, b)` produces `a, a+1, ..., b-1` - it always stops one short of `b`.

## What it looks like when it goes wrong

A loop that should include the last number doesn't, because `range(1, n)` stops at `n - 1`.

## How to spot it

Print out `list(range(a, b))` for small numbers and check what's actually in it.

## How to fix it

Use `range(a, b + 1)` when you need `b` included.

## Try it

```python run
print(list(range(1, 5)))
print(list(range(1, 6)))
```

concepts.title: Recursion and base cases
concepts.summary: Every recursive function needs a condition where it stops calling itself.
concepts.lesson_md:
## What it is

A recursive function calls itself with a smaller version of the problem, until a base case stops the chain.

## What it looks like when it goes wrong

```
RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
```

## How to spot it

Check the function for a condition that returns *without* calling itself again - and check every recursive call actually moves towards that condition.

## How to fix it

Add the missing base case, or fix the recursive call so it genuinely gets closer to it each time.

## Try it

```python run
def count_down(n):
    if n <= 0:
        print("Done!")
        return
    print(n)
    count_down(n - 1)

count_down(3)
```

concepts.title: Dividing by zero (and guarding against it)
concepts.summary: Check a count isn't zero before you divide by it.
concepts.lesson_md:
## What it is

Dividing (or using %) by zero always crashes in Python, so any value you divide by needs to be checked first if it could be zero.

## What it looks like when it goes wrong

```
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
```

## How to spot it

Look at what's on the right of `/` or `%` - could it ever be zero? An empty list's length is the classic case.

## How to fix it

Add a guard: check the value before dividing, and decide what should happen in that empty case instead of crashing.

## Try it

```python run
scores = []
if len(scores) == 0:
    print("No scores yet")
else:
    print(sum(scores) / len(scores))
```

puzzles.title: Colon Needed
puzzles.brief_md:
`is_even(n)` should return `True` if `n` is even, and `False` otherwise.

Example: `is_even(4)` should return `True`. `is_even(7)` should return `False`.

hints.hint_md: This code won't even run yet - look at the error message before you think about logic at all.
Look closely at the `def` line. Every line that opens a block needs something specific at the end.
Add a colon `:` at the end of the `def is_even(n)` line.

bugs.what_md: The `def` line has no colon, so Python can't tell where the function's body is supposed to start.
bugs.fix_md: Add `:` after the closing parenthesis: `def is_even(n):`.

puzzles.explanation_md: Every block header in Python - `def`, `if`, `for`, `while`, `class`, and the rest - ends with a colon. Without it, Python's parser doesn't know an indented block is coming next, and it fails before running a single line of your code.
puzzles.spot_it_md: Before you run anything, scan every line that should open a block and check it ends in `:`.

puzzles.title: Mystery Name
puzzles.brief_md:
`greet(name)` should return a greeting like `"Hello, Ada!"`.

Example: `greet("Ada")` should return `"Hello, Ada!"`.

hints.hint_md: The code runs and then crashes - that's a `NameError`. Read the traceback's last line first.
Look at the variable used inside the message. Compare its spelling to the function's parameter.
`nmae` should be `name` - fix the typo so it matches the parameter exactly.

bugs.what_md: `nmae` is never defined - it's a typo for the parameter `name`, so Python raises a `NameError` the moment this line runs.

puzzles.explanation_md: Python only recognises a name once it's been created - it doesn't guess what you meant. A typo in a variable name looks right to the eye but is a completely different, undefined name to Python, so it crashes as soon as that line runs.
puzzles.spot_it_md: When you see a `NameError`, compare the named variable letter-by-letter against where it was created.

puzzles.title: The Missing Number
puzzles.brief_md:
`sum_to(n)` should return the sum of all whole numbers from 1 up to and including `n`.

Example: `sum_to(4)` should return `10` (1 + 2 + 3 + 4).
puzzles.predict_prompt_md: What do you think `sum_to(4)` returns? Write it down before you run anything.

hints.hint_md: The code runs without errors, so this is a logic bug. Compare your result for `sum_to(4)` with 10.
Look at the `range()` call. Which numbers does `range(1, n)` actually produce?
`range` stops one short of its second value. You need the loop to reach `n` itself.

bugs.what_md: `range(1, n)` stops at `n - 1`, so `n` is never added.

puzzles.explanation_md: Python's `range(a, b)` includes `a` but excludes `b` - it's a deliberate design choice that trips almost everyone up at least once. Whenever a loop should include the upper value, add one to the second argument.
puzzles.spot_it_md: Any time you loop with `range`, check the first and last values by hand with a tiny input like `n = 1` or `n = 2`.

puzzles.title: Infinite Descent
puzzles.brief_md:
`factorial(n)` should return `n!` (n factorial): `n * (n-1) * (n-2) * ... * 1`.

Example: `factorial(5)` should return `120`. By definition, `factorial(0)` and `factorial(1)` both return `1`.
puzzles.predict_prompt_md: What do you think happens when you run `factorial(5)`? Will it finish? Write down what you expect before you run it.

hints.hint_md: This one crashes with a `RecursionError` - the function keeps calling itself and never stops.
Every recursive function needs a condition where it stops calling itself. Does this one have one?
Add a base case: if `n <= 1`, return `1` directly, before the recursive call.

bugs.what_md: There's no base case, so `factorial` keeps calling itself with a smaller `n` forever, until Python's recursion limit is hit.
bugs.fix_md: Add `if n <= 1: return 1` before the recursive call.

puzzles.explanation_md: Recursive functions need two things: a base case that returns without recursing, and a recursive case that's guaranteed to move closer to that base case. This function only has the recursive case, so it never stops - it just keeps calling itself with smaller and smaller numbers until Python gives up.
puzzles.spot_it_md: Whenever you write a recursive function, write the base case first and check the recursive call actually moves towards it.

puzzles.title: Grade Calculator
puzzles.brief_md:
`calculate_grade(scores)` takes a list of test scores (0-100) and returns a grade:

- `"Distinction"` if the average is 70 or above
- `"Pass"` if the average is 50 or above (but below 70)
- `"Fail"` otherwise
- `"No scores"` if the list is empty

Example: `calculate_grade([85, 90, 95])` should return `"Distinction"`.

tests.label: calculate_grade([70, 70, 70]) - exactly on the Distinction boundary
calculate_grade([50, 50, 50]) - exactly on the Pass boundary

hints.hint_md: Try scores that land exactly on 50 or 70, and try an empty list - does the brief's boundary wording match what the code actually does?
There are two separate problems here: what happens with no scores at all, and what happens exactly on a grade boundary.
Guard against an empty list before dividing, and use `>=` instead of `>` so a score exactly on the boundary gets the higher grade.

bugs.what_md: If `scores` is empty, `len(scores)` is `0` and dividing by it crashes with a `ZeroDivisionError`.
bugs.fix_md: Check for an empty list first and return `"No scores"` before dividing.

bugs.what_md: Using `>` instead of `>=` means a score landing exactly on a boundary (70 or 50) is marked down a grade.
bugs.fix_md: Change both comparisons to `>=` so the boundary itself counts for the higher grade.

puzzles.explanation_md: Two separate bugs here. First, dividing by `len(scores)` crashes on an empty list because there's no guard for that case. Second, `>` silently excludes the boundary value itself - the brief says "70 or above", which means `>=`, not `>`. Neither bug stops the other from being tested, so fixing one doesn't reveal the other automatically - you need to check both the empty case and the exact boundaries.
puzzles.spot_it_md: For any function with thresholds, test the exact boundary values by hand, and always ask what happens with an empty or missing input.
